sections.title: How wounds heal
blocks: Wounds heal in **overlapping phases** over months.

mech.t: Neutrophils and macrophages clean the wound (days 1–4); mild redness is normal.
Fibroblasts lay down collagen and new vessels; epithelium covers the wound (days 4–21).
Collagen reorganises and strengthens over 12–18 months.

sections.title: Clinical features
blocks: Keep the dressing on and **dry for 24–48 h**, then gently wash and pat dry. A thin layer of **plain petroleum jelly** keeps the wound moist (no routine topical antibiotics: they cause allergy (neomycin, bacitracin) and resistance). For scalp and posterior neck, keep the hair clean.
Absorbable deep sutures (e.g. poliglecaprone; the course Monocryl) dissolve over weeks. Surface nylon (Ethilon) is removed at the times above.

ul: **Avoid strenuous exercise, heavy lifting, contact sport and swimming for ~1–2 weeks** (until sutures are out and the wound is sound) to prevent **dehiscence and stretched scars**. course teaching said no football for 2 weeks.

**Work:** a construction worker may need **1–2 weeks of modified or light duties**. The fit note (from any eligible healthcare professional, including pharmacists since July 2022) can advise "may be fit for work with adjustments".
Protect the wound from dust and dirt at work (a waterproof dressing).
**Massage** with emollient once healed (from about 2–3 weeks).
**Sun protection (SPF 30+) for at least a year** to avoid pigmentation.
**Silicone gel or sheets** for hypertrophic-scar-prone patients (OTC/prescribable).

**Keloids:** specialist intralesional triamcinolone (hypopigmentation and atrophy are possible), pressure, cryotherapy, or radiotherapy after excision. **Avoid elective surgery on high-risk sites** in keloid formers.

sections.title: Management

ul: **Signs:** increasing pain, redness spreading **>1–2 cm** from the edge, swelling; **pus**, wound breakdown; fever
Mild stitch-line redness in the first 48 h is normal.

**Management (NICE NG125/NG141 principles, local formulary):** swab if there is discharge; **flucloxacillin** first-line for *S. aureus*/streptococci; **penicillin allergy: clarithromycin or doxycycline**, but check **warfarin/DOAC interactions** and **statins** (clarithromycin with simvastatin is contraindicated; hold the statin); remove sutures if there is an abscess; same-day review if systemically unwell

blocks: The IP can prescribe analgesia (paracetamol), treat confirmed wound infection, advise on dressings and silicone, issue fit notes, and **check the INR** after interacting antibiotics. Review isotretinoin/acitretin users' wound healing.

refer.t: Spreading redness, fever, pus or increasing pain after surgery: assess for **wound infection or abscess** the same day.

sections.title: Red flags and when to refer

ul: Spreading redness, fever, pus or increasing pain after surgery: assess for **wound infection or abscess** the same day.
Infection, dehiscence, haematoma, hypertrophic scar or keloid.

pearls: Give written aftercare with a **named contact for bleeding/infection** and the **date for suture removal and results**.

quiz.q: When should you think of Wound aftercare: sutures, activity, infection & scars?
quiz.a: A patient a few days to weeks after minor skin surgery with a question about the wound, stitches, activity or scar.
Healing goes through inflammation, proliferation and remodelling; tension and infection disrupt it; some people form keloids.

quiz.q: What is the backbone of care?
quiz.a: Keep dry 24–48 h then wash; sutures out at 5–7 days on the face, 10–14 on the trunk and arms and about 14 on the back and legs (local protocols vary); avoid strenuous activity for 1–2 weeks; flucloxacillin for wound infection (clarithromycin or doxycycline if penicillin-allergic, checking interactions).
Spreading cellulitis, abscess, dehiscence; keloids in people with skin of colour or on the chest, shoulders and earlobes.
